questions.q: What does `git merge feature-login` do while on `main`?
options: Deletes feature-login after combining it
Rewrites every commit on feature-login with new hashes
Creates a new merge commit with both branch tips as parents, without rewriting any existing commits
Renames main to feature-login
questions.explain: Merge ties two histories together with a new commit; it never rewrites commits that already exist.

questions.q: Why do commits replayed by `git rebase` get new commit hashes, even when the code changes are identical?
options: Because rebase deletes the original commits and writes brand-new commits with a different base, which changes the hash
Git randomly reassigns hashes for no reason
Rebase doesn't actually change hashes — this is a myth
Hashes only change if you add the --force flag
questions.explain: A commit's hash is derived partly from its parent commit, so replaying it onto a different base necessarily produces a new commit with a new hash.

questions.q: What is the one hard rule about using `git rebase`?
options: Never use rebase on a Friday
Rebase can only be used on the main branch
Rebase requires a paid GitHub plan
Never rebase a branch that other people have already pulled and are building on top of
questions.explain: Rewriting shared history creates a mismatch between your new commits and what others already have, which is genuinely painful to untangle.

questions.q: According to the practical default in this lesson, when should you reach for merge rather than rebase?
options: Never — rebase should always be used instead
When combining a finished, shared branch back into main — the same action a pull request's merge button performs
Only when working entirely offline
Only on branches with fewer than two commits
questions.explain: Merge is the right call once a branch is shared/finished and being folded back into main, which is exactly what a PR merge does.

questions.q: What does a "linear history" (the result of rebasing) mean, compared to one produced by repeated merging?
options: A history that only has one single commit total
A history that cannot be viewed with git log
A history with no branch-and-join shape — commits appear in one straight sequence instead of diverging and rejoining
A history stored on a different server
questions.explain: Rebase replays commits onto a single line, avoiding the extra merge-commit branch points that repeated merging produces.
